catalog_quote: The following is the maximal projection of Chung syllable structure. However, some Chung words have a sesqui-syllabic structure (Matisoff 1973), initiated with an unstressed minor syllable, of CV structure, followed by a stressed, major syllable, which has either a CVC, CVV, CCVV, or a CCVVC structure. [...] CV/Cəŋ This structure is not realized independently; it usually occurs in the pre-syllable position in sesqui-syllabic words. [...] Sesqui-syllabic Words. These are a type of disyllabic words where main, stressed syllables are preceded by minor, unstressed pre-syllables. The vowel of the pre-syllable is usually written as the neutralized vowel [ə]. CV.CVV pəsii 'snake' CV.CVC /pəsom/ 'star' CV.CVVC /kətooŋ/ 'six' CV.CCVC /kəmlɔh/ 'young man' CV.CCVVC cəkruuk 'basket'. There is no contrast between CV and CVV in identical environments. [p. 50] Chung is a non-tonal language. However, there are 4 suprasegmental phonemes based on the contrastive use of phonation types, namely clear or modal voice, creaky voice, breathy voice, and breathy-creaky voice. [...] The following are different notations of each register whose features are mostly carried by the nucleus, or vowel, of the main syllable. There is no register contrast in minor, or unstressed, syllables. [p. 49] There are no occurrences of short vowels in open stressed syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Sa'och (Chung) is non-tonal with four phonation registers; native words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables, and stress falls on the major (main) syllable, i.e. the final syllable; any preceding minor syllable (CV with a neutralized vowel [ə]) is unstressed and carries no register contrast. Stress is thus predictable (non-contrastive), always on the word-final full syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Related remarks: 'There is no register contrast in minor, or unstressed, syllables' (p. 50); 'There are no occurrences of short vowels in open stressed syllables' (p. 49); the pre-syllable vowel is neutralized to [ə]; Chung Yuy tends to simplify or drop the pre-syllable altogether (pp. 62-63, 94-95).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: phonological description of the Chung (Sa'och) word in citation forms; the thesis covers both Chung Yuy (Thung Na village, Kanchanaburi, Thailand) and Chung Yul (Veal Renh, Prey Nob district, Kampong Som, Cambodia). Statement is about monosyllables and sesqui-syllables (the only native word shapes described; polysyllabic loans from Thai/Khmer are not treated for stress).
new_statements.identity_note: Isara 2007 calls the language 'Chung' (autonym [tɕʰṳˀŋ]); 'Saoch' is the Khmer exonym. The thesis describes both varieties of saoc1239: Chung Yuy (Thung Na village, Kanchanaburi, Thailand; descendants of 1830s war captives) and Chung Yul (Veal Renh, Prey Nob district, Kampong Som / Preah Sihanouk, Cambodia); the syllable/stress statement is given for 'Chung' generally, with the varieties differing only in pre-syllable complexity (Chung Yuy simplifies or drops the pre-syllable). Glottolog lists no dialect children under saoc1239. The Headley 1985 statement is genus-level (Pearic) but explicitly includes 'Saoch of Veal Renh' among its dialects.

new_statements.quote: There are 9 short vowels and 9 long vowels in Chung. There are no occurrences of short vowels in open stressed syllables. In other words, there is no contrast of short and long vowels in open syllables. [p. 73, sec. 2.2] ... Chung is a non-tonal language. However, there are 4 suprasegmental phonemic contrasts based on the use of three "phonation types", namely clear (modal) voice, creaky voice, breathy voice, and the combination breathy-creaky voice, which are similar to Chong, another Pearic language spoken in Thailand (Isara 2002). These suprasegmentals are called 'registers' in this study. [p. 73, sec. 2.3] ... It is remarkable that in the case of Chung Yul, pre-syllable structure is more complex and varied, while it is rather simple in Chung Yuy, which has /kə-/ as pre-syllable in almost all cases. [p. 74, sec. 3.2]

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's fixed: final syllable record and with the existing Isara 2007 statement (unstressed minor CV pre-syllable followed by a stressed major syllable). The 2009 paper is a condensation of that thesis: it repeats the 'no short vowels in open stressed syllables' restriction (thesis p. 49) and the non-tonal / four-register statement (thesis p. 50) but drops the explicit sesqui-syllabic stress sentence. It adds nothing new on placement, secondary stress or exceptions; it does not contradict anything.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The paper has no stress section and never states where stress falls. It presupposes a stressed/unstressed distinction (short vowels are barred from open stressed syllables), says the language is non-tonal with four phonation-type registers, and describes words as a reduced pre-syllable (Chung Yuy almost always /kə-/) plus a main syllable, i.e. the Mon-Khmer sesqui-syllable inherited 'as a Mon-Khmer feature' (p. 82). Stress on the main, word-final syllable is therefore implicit in the frame the author uses, not stated; the explicit statement is in the same author's 2007 thesis, which the catalog already cites.
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress. Diphthongs [iə, ɯə, uə] occur only in Thai/Khmer loans (p. 73); Chung Yuy tends to drop the pre-syllable altogether, 'a move towards mono-syllabicity' (p. 83), which would leave such words monosyllabic.
new_statements.identity_note: The paper covers both varieties, Chung Yuy (Thailand, Thung Na, Kanchanaburi) and Chung Yul (Cambodia, Veal Renh, Kampong Som), and introduces those names (sec. 3, p. 74); its phonological inventory (sec. 2) is given for Chung as a whole, with dialect differences confined to clusters, pre-syllables and finals (sec. 3). Chung Yul's more varied pre-syllables are said to preserve the inherited sesqui-syllabic shape; Chung Yuy simplifies pre-syllables to /kə-/ or drops them under Thai contact.
